headline: Democrats' gains, a Brampton plant fight and Nvidia's CEO exit mark the week
summary: Democrats added a Mississippi Senate seat and the Kansas governorship to their midterm sweep, while hopes for an Iran deal rose and then faded, sending oil back toward US$96. In Ontario, Stellantis's sale of the Brampton plant set off a confrontation with Ottawa that may end in court, and the province named powerful new regional chairs. Nvidia's Jensen Huang resigned, and a Microsoft email outage disrupted Toronto hospitals and schools.

top.headline: Democrats' sweep grows with Mississippi Senate and Kansas governor wins
top.what: Democrat Scott Colom was projected the winner over Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith on Wednesday and she conceded, and the Associated Press called the Kansas governor's race for Democrat Cindy Holscher on Thursday. Alaska is the last uncalled Senate race.
top.why: Control of Congress changes in January, which affects tariffs, oversight of the White House and U.S. policy toward Canada.

top.headline: Iran deal hopes fade as Trump says none is needed; oil rebounds
top.what: Brent dipped below US$90 on Tuesday on hopes for a deal, then settled at US$95.82 on Thursday after Trump said the U.S. needs no agreement and pulled Vance off the talks. Iran reported tankers hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz, and Israel's cabinet reportedly ordered readiness for a strike.
top.why: Oil prices drive gas costs and inflation in Canada, and with them the Bank of Canada's next rate move.

top.headline: Ottawa and Stellantis head toward court over Brampton plant sale
top.what: Stellantis announced the sale of its idled Brampton plant to armoured-vehicle maker Roshel on Monday. By Thursday Ottawa had started a 30-day default clock, rejected a $24-million repayment offer and threatened to sue, while facing questions about what it knew beforehand.
top.why: About 1,800 laid-off GTA auto workers and hundreds of millions in public subsidies are at stake.

top.headline: Nvidia's Jensen Huang resigns amid reports of a Chinese intelligence link
top.what: Huang quit as chief executive on Thursday after reports about a relationship with a woman U.S. officials reportedly believe worked for Chinese intelligence; finance chief Colette Kress is interim CEO and lawmakers want him to testify.
top.why: Nvidia is among the most widely held stocks in Canadian pension and index funds, and the case may tighten U.S. chip export rules.

top.headline: Ontario names 'strong chairs' for eight regions, including York and Peel
top.what: The province appointed regional heads with powers to veto some bylaws, propose budgets and hire or fire senior staff, among them Vaughan Mayor Steven Del Duca in York; several mayors and a replaced chair objected.
top.why: The appointees, not voters, now steer budgets and property-tax decisions across most of the GTA from Nov. 15.

top.headline: Microsoft email outage hits Toronto hospitals, schools and City Hall
top.what: An Outlook failure on Thursday led Unity Health Toronto to declare a Code Grey and disrupted universities, City Hall and VIA Rail; repairs continued into Friday with no confirmed cause.
top.why: It showed how many essential services depend on a single company's online email.

top.headline: U.S. envoys meet Putin, then Zelenskyy; Europe to join next round
top.what: Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met Putin in Moscow and briefed Zelenskyy near Dublin on Thursday without a breakthrough, but agreed European countries will join the next round of talks.
top.why: A settlement, or its failure, shapes European security, defence spending and Canada's commitments to Ukraine.

top.headline: Ontario plans OSAP caps for private career colleges as aid freeze drags on
top.what: After student walkouts over aid and tuition, the province on Thursday outlined a bill to cap OSAP-funded enrolment at private colleges and bar mostly-online programs; the freeze on aid at those colleges continues.
top.why: Thousands of Ontario students are waiting on aid they need to stay enrolled.
